title: Project H.O.M.E.
program: Community Living, Retail, Educational, Hydroponics, Recreational Facilities
body: The built environment is a set of vast interconnected systems.

HOME stands for housing, ownership, mentorship and education. The project designs a system rather than a set of buildings, treating affordable housing as a means rather than an end. Through housing, mentorship and education, the aim is to shorten a decades-long route out of poverty to less than a decade, which meant rethinking the role affordable housing plays in the American housing market.

The housing is planned closer to a college dormitory than an apartment building. Combining kitchen, living, bathing and study space reduces cost, and each person or family holds a private room or a pair of connected rooms. Shared space builds the social habits usually formed at college, but the residents are not students, so the layout aims for community without uniformity. A split-level arrangement produced what I called a village in a building: rooms and shared amenities separated by an outdoor network of paths, stairs and planting, with space for residents to make their own entrances.

Income to subsidize the housing has to come from what the surrounding area lacks. In Mantua, that was fresh produce and commercial space. Indoor hydroponic farming generates substantial income from produce sold into the city, employs residents, and teaches them a growing trade. With rent from commercial space and smaller operations across the site, the system covers its own costs and funds social workers, teachers and other support for residents.

The architecture is a representation of the system it serves. Treating a building as a machine is not new, but doing so at a systemic level, with what we now know about design, could address problems not usually considered architectural.
